areas.name: Mount Vaux
areas.blurb: Mount Vaux is the northernmost big peak of the Ottertail Range in Yoho National Park, rising above the Trans-Canada Highway and the Hanbury Glacier. It was first climbed in 1901 and is still lightly visited.

areas.name: Mount Begbie
areas.blurb: Mount Begbie is the landmark peak of the Gold Range in the Monashee Mountains, rising above Revelstoke on the Columbia River. A steep forest trail leads to a small glacier below its north ridge.

areas.name: Brunswick Mountain
areas.blurb: Brunswick Mountain tops every other summit in the North Shore Mountains, standing above Lions Bay on Howe Sound. It is a strenuous day from the village and is also reached from the Howe Sound Crest Trail.

areas.name: Ossa Mountain
areas.blurb: Ossa Mountain is a 2,261 m summit in the Tantalus Range northwest of Squamish, with views across the Sunshine Coast ranges and Mount Tantalus. It is the more reachable of the Tantalus peaks, with a scramble as its easiest route.

routes.name: Southwest Face
routes.rock_grade: Steep ledge wall about 15 m high below the summit block; difficult scrambling, with loose rubble throughout
routes.best_season: Late summer, once the lower gully is snow-free and the upper snow ridge is passable. The lower drainage is a hot west-facing gully with little water.
routes.overview: The southwest face route follows a single long drainage straight up from the highway, with no trail. Loose rubble and a steep wall of small ledges below the summit block make it harder than most scrambles. It is a big day with over 2,000 m of gain.
routes.beta: Cross the logged area from the roadside, enter a shallow canyon and follow it up onto the wide avalanche slope. Continue up the long drainage, which becomes steep, loose rubble. Reach a snow ridge and then the crux wall of small ledges below the summit block; some parties roped here. Above it, traverse steep rubble diagonally, following cairns, to a short rubbly ridge and the top.
routes.approach: Park at the tiny roadside pull-out off the Trans-Canada Highway below the southwest face. There is no trail; begin through shrubs and rubble on the lower avalanche slopes.
routes.descent_text: Descend the same route, downclimbing the crux wall carefully, then glissade or plunge-step snow patches and descend the long loose rubble of the lower gully.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if snow on the ridge is too hard to cross safely or if water and daylight are running low in the heat.
routes.bail: Retreat down the drainage, spreading out horizontally to limit rockfall on partners.

pitch_detail.notes: Logged area, shallow canyon and avalanche slope; fill water here.
Steep, very loose rubble slopes to a snow ridge.
Wall of small ledges, about 15 m, with exposure and loose rock; some parties rope up.
Diagonal traverse on steep rubble to a short ridge and the top.

routes.watch_out:
Never stay directly above or below partners
Water is scarce above the lower drainage
pro_tips: Start early to beat the heat on the west-facing gully
Fill water at the last reliable flow low on the route

approach_logistics.trailhead: Trans-Canada Highway roadside pull-out below the southwest face

routes.name: North Ridge via North Glacier
routes.rock_grade: Fourth-class step on loose rock to reach the ledge; ledge is narrow and exposed; the north ridge is easy on quartzite
routes.best_season: Mid-July to mid-September, when the lower slabs are dry. As the glacier has shrunk, the ledge access has become harder.
routes.overview: A steep forest trail leads to a campsite at tree line, then the route crosses a small crevassed glacier to an exposed ledge that gives onto the easy north ridge. The ridge ends at a snow wall with a cornice near the top.
routes.beta: From the campsite, go up alpine slabs to the glacier and cross it, watching for crevasses. Reach the ledge on the east side of the glacier; the step up to it is fourth class on loose rock, and the ledge is narrow and exposed, with bolt anchors that allow a handline. Beyond the ledge the north ridge is easy scrambling on solid quartzite to a final snow wall and cornice below the summit.
routes.approach: Drive south from Revelstoke on Highway 23 about 10 km to the gravel parking lot just south of the Begbie Creek bridge. A steep trail climbs through old forest to a treeline camp with tent platforms and a toilet; the glacier starts about a kilometre beyond it.
routes.descent_text: The usual descent goes down the east ridge on rock and steep snow to the col, then a steep north couloir to the glacier. Parties also rappel from the ledge anchors.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if you cannot protect the glacier crossing or the ledge, or if the weather turns.
routes.bail: Retreat the way you came: back across the ledge (rappel from the bolts) and down the glacier.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep switchbacks through forest to tree line, about 1,830 m.
Alpine slabs then a small crevassed glacier.
Fourth-class step on loose rock to a narrow, exposed ledge; handline or rappel anchors.
Easy ridge to a snow wall and cornice below the summit.

what_to_bring: Camping gear if staying at tree line
hazards: Crevasses on a heavily crevassed small glacier
Moat or bergschrund at the glacier edge
routes.watch_out: The glacier has shrunk, making the ledge access harder than older descriptions
pro_tips: Bring full crampons rather than microspikes
Consider camping at tree line to split the day

access.land_manager: BC Parks and Recreation Sites and Trails BC

approach_logistics.trailhead: Mount Begbie trailhead, Highway 23 south of Revelstoke

routes.name: Lions Bay Trail
routes.rock_grade: Steep, loose ground with Class 3 sections on the last kilometre
routes.best_season: Summer to early fall. In snow or ice the exposed upper ridge needs crampons and an axe, and the guidance is not to continue without them.
routes.overview: A steep route from Lions Bay that climbs old service roads and forest to a vista point, then a very steep final ridge with Class 3 scrambling to the summit. The last stretch near the top is narrow and exposed.
routes.beta: Follow the gravel service road, go left at the Mt. Brunswick sign, cross Magnesia Creek and keep right, then climb switchbacks to the end of the road at a viewpoint. From there the route climbs the steep ridge; the final kilometre has Class 3 sections, and about half a kilometre below the top is exposed and steep. The true summit lies beyond a saddle.
routes.approach: Drive to the end of Sunset Drive North, off the Lions Bay exit of the Sea to Sky Highway.
routes.descent_text: Return by the same route down the ridge and service roads.
routes.turnaround: Turn back in bad weather or if the upper ridge holds snow or ice and you lack crampons.
routes.bail: Retreat the way you came; the upper ridge is steep and loose.

pitch_detail.notes: Very steep final kilometre with Class 3 sections, loose rock, and an exposed narrow stretch.

gear: Helmet if climbing in a group
hazards: Steep exposed ridge near the top
Snow and ice in the cold months
routes.watch_out: A slip on the narrow summit ridge could be serious
pro_tips: Start early; it is a big day
Skip the summit push in poor weather

approach_logistics.trailhead: Lions Bay, end of Sunset Drive North

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.rock_grade: Class 4 scrambling with a downclimb into a notch and a chimney crux near the top
routes.best_season: Midsummer to early fall, once snow has melted off the upper mountain; any glacier cover on the trail calls for crampons and an axe.
routes.overview: Ossa Mountain is climbed by its east ridge, a long day from the Squamish side with steep forest, meadows and creek crossings below a route-finding scramble. Near the top the route downclimbs into a notch and works through a chimney section before the summit.
routes.beta: Climb steeply through forest and meadows, crossing creeks, to the upper mountain. The upper scramble is hard to follow: expect route-finding, a downclimb into a notch, and a crux in chimneys. Plenty of water is available lower down.
routes.descent_text: Return the same way; the downclimbs and loose ground make the descent as serious as the ascent.
hazards: Snow or glacier cover early in the season
gear: Ice axe and crampons if snow or ice remains

approach_logistics.trailhead: Ossa Mountain trailhead, about 30 minutes from Squamish
